articleTitle: Intelligent consumer products-past, present and future
publicationTitle: 1992 IEE Colloquium on Intelligent Consumer Products (Digest No: 1992/013)
abstract: The last 20 years have seen a major change in the design and operation of consumer products as well as the introduction of new products. The driving force behind each of these developments has been the increasing availability at reducing the real cost of electronics and associating processing power. This has enabled the introduction of higher levels of control and increased functionality into what were primarily mechanical systems and has also resulted in a range of totally new products which would not be achievable by any other means. The results of incorporating electronics and associated software has therefore been to produce a range of consumer products which are inherently 'mechatronic' in nature, placing demands upon their designers to achieve high levels of integration between the electronic, mechanical and software elements in their construction. In order to understand the developments that have taken place as a result of the introduction of electronics, the development of a particular and common consumer product, namely the washing machine, is considered.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: 1992 IEE Colloquium on Intelligent Consumer Products (Digest No: 1992/013)
abstract: Consumer electronic products are often not only difficult to use, but it seems also that much less progress is being made by manufacturers in interface design than in styling or technology or low-cost manufacture. What is it about designing easy-to-use products that is so difficult-and why does so little of the research seem to reach the High Street? This paper explores these issues from a view of the consumer product development process and asserts that there is an urgent need for a rapid user interface prototyping tool to be used in the initial concept phase of a project. The requirements of such a tool are described, concluding with a demonstration of the system developed and used by Cambridge Consultants.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: 1992 IEE Colloquium on Intelligent Consumer Products (Digest No: 1992/013)
abstract: Deals with the practical design of a range of intelligent products. Triton, a key customer, approached Turnright Controls in December 1990 with a view to launching new products at the Interbuild Exhibition, November 1991. Interbuild is held only every two years, and this dictated a ten month design timescale. This is a semi-technical topic dealing with the design of a particular product by a manufacturer, helped by an example of how a specific product (Spabath and instant heat shower ranges) was designed and tested, giving details of problems encountered from a manufacturer/designer's perspective.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: 1992 IEE Colloquium on Intelligent Consumer Products (Digest No: 1992/013)
abstract: Badly designed interactive systems can handicap users, who are usually blamed by manufacturers for their own difficulties. ('Users should read the manual first', they say). This attitude not only hinders users but turns attention from the engineering design of interfaces to the psychology of usability. The author argues, with examples, that there is ample scope for the improvement of interfaces through better engineering.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Technolust versus creative design: some implications of 'intelligent' products for design
publicationTitle: 1992 IEE Colloquium on Intelligent Consumer Products (Digest No: 1992/013)
abstract: The increase in technological power available to designers and engineers as a result of advances in 'intelligent' product technology provides new challenges to all involved. This is particularly important within the cultural dimension of design, where more can be said about a product than just that it works well from a technological, financial, ergonomic, and marketing point of view. This paper outlines salient issues from the viewpoint of a member of the Chartered Society of Designers.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
